title: In the Sistine Chapel a pope needs two thirds of the votes: in May 2025, 89 of 133
body: A pope is elected only in the Sistine Chapel, and only by cardinals who were under 80 when the see fell vacant: in May 2025, 133 of the 135 who qualified. Each writes one name on a card headed *Eligo in Summum Pontificem* (I elect as Supreme Pontiff), in a disguised hand, and three scrutineers read every vote aloud. Under [Universi Dominici Gregis](https://www.vatican.va/content/john-paul-ii/en/apost_constitutions/documents/hf_jp-ii_apc_22021996_universi-dominici-gregis.html), the rules of 1996, a winner needs **two thirds** of the electors voting: 89 of 133. So any 45 can block a candidate, and no faction wins without others. Those rules also let the cardinals switch to a simple majority after 33 or 34 ballots; the author Paul Collins warned that this could encourage a small majority to hold out. On 11 June 2007 Pope Benedict XVI restored two thirds for every ballot. After each morning and afternoon of voting the cards are burned, and chemicals turn the smoke black, or white for a new pope. On 8 May 2025 white smoke rose at 6:07 p.m. after the fourth ballot: Robert Francis Prevost had become Pope Leo XIV.

slides.question: In May 2025 the cardinals could vote up to four times a day. How many ballots did it take to elect a pope?
slides.explanation: 4: one on the evening of 7 May and three on 8 May, two in the morning and the fourth in the afternoon, when white smoke rose at 6:07 p.m.

slides.alt: Animation in scarlet and ivory on dark red: 133 cardinals fill a plan of the Sistine Chapel; a ballot card, Eligo in Summum Pontificem, folded into an urn; scrutineers and a needle and thread; 89 of 133 seats lit gold; the 1996 rule; a stove and black and white smoke; Leo XIV.
slides.music: “I Can Feel it Coming” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Back one candidate with groups of cardinals until he reaches two thirds. Then switch to the 1996 rule for late ballots and win with just two groups.
slides.takeaway: No two of these groups reach 89, so three of the four must agree. Under the 1996 rule’s late majority of 67, the biggest group and any other were enough, once 34 ballots had passed.

slides.alt: Photo looking up between Vatican buildings: on the left the tall, plain brick wall of the Sistine Chapel with small arched windows near the top; on the right a small dome and, behind it, the great grey dome of St Peter’s Basilica under a pale sky.
slides.caption: The Sistine Chapel (left), a plain brick box outside, beside the dome of St Peter’s Basilica. In a conclave the smoke rises from a stovepipe on its roof.

slides.heading: One ballot in the Sistine Chapel

steps.label: Write one name, in a disguised hand
Fold it, swear an oath, put it in the urn
Three scrutineers read every name aloud
A needle threads each card through Eligo
The cards burn: black or white smoke

left.label: 1996 to 2007
left.text: Two thirds for the first 33 or 34 ballots. Then a majority could switch to a simple majority: 67 of 133.

right.label: Since 2007
right.text: Two thirds for every ballot. In the end only the two leading names stay in, and since 2013 those two may not vote.

slides.question: In the conclave of May 2025, 133 cardinals voted. How many of them, voting for others, could stop any candidate from winning?
slides.explanation: 45: then a candidate gets at most 88 votes, one short of the 89 needed, two thirds of 133. With a simple majority, 67 votes would be needed and 67 could block.
